output.brief:
The enrolment drop is mostly a yield problem, not an applicant-quality problem. Applications, admits and GPA all rose. Yield fell only in the Dean's and Merit award tiers, whose awards were cut from $14,000 to $9,000 and from $9,000 to $5,000. Yield in the Presidential tier (award unchanged) and the no-award group barely moved. Early-action admits were handled on the old system with an on-time timetable, yet their yield fell by about the same amount (45.2% to 37.8%) as regular decision (39.0% to 31.5%). So the late portal-era decisions do not explain the main drop, although individual students like the Westcombe one were probably lost to delay. The scholarship cut explains the drop far better. The finance committee expected little yield effect, using a 2021 elasticity estimate.

Do not replace the Director. That would punish the wrong party and leave the cause in place. Take a proposal to the finance committee to restore awards in the Dean's and Merit tiers, with the revenue trade-off modelled, before award letters go out. Also set a monthly regular-decision turnaround target. Hold off on the vendor rebuild until the missing-transcript claims are checked. I am fairly confident in this. The remaining gap is how much each of the two causes of the regular-decision delay (reader cuts versus the late scoring module) contributed.
output.methodChoice: Collected X8 (yield by tier) and X10 (yield by round) as the items most able to separate the scholarship, portal-delay and general-demand explanations.
